note: Client-safe short source windows for academy foundation sessions. Hebrew and translations are excerpts already used in this repo (seed lessons, curriculum snippets, or public-domain Hebrew plus a short educational gloss), so a learner can answer on the page. Sefaria links are secondary. Do not treat this as a full text store. Teach-before-ask: excerpts may show terms; asks stay plain until taught.

Genesis 1:1.hebrew: בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ
Genesis 1:1.translation: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
Genesis 1:1.setting: Opening verse of the Torah — a narrative line, not a rule or a debate.

Genesis 1:1–2:3.hebrew: בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ
Genesis 1:1–2:3.translation: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
Genesis 1:1–2:3.setting: The first creation account runs from this opening verse through the close of the seventh day.

Genesis 22.translation: He said to him, “Abraham,” and he said, “Here I am.”
Genesis 22.setting: A narrative line from the binding of Isaac — a named actor answers a call.

Deuteronomy 6:4.hebrew: שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ ה׳ אֶחָד
Deuteronomy 6:4.translation: Hear, Israel: the Lord is our God, the Lord is one.
Deuteronomy 6:4.setting: A Torah verse of direct address — later reused in prayer, but first a verse.

Psalm 23.translation: The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not lack.
Psalm 23.setting: A psalm line of image and trust — poetry, not a legal ruling.

Job 38-40.translation: God answers Job with a long series of questions.
Job 38-40.setting: A questioning speech from the book of Job — the form is inquiry, whether or not a tidy answer follows.

Job 42.hebrew: ה׳ נָתַן וַה׳ לָקָח יְהִי שֵׁם ה׳ מְבֹרָךְ
Job 42.translation: The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.
Job 42.setting: A short Job window already used in Academy thought sessions — the book later restores Job’s fortunes while leaving the deeper question of suffering open.

Mishnah Berakhot 1:1.translation: From when do we recite Shema in the evening?
Mishnah Berakhot 1:1.setting: A compact Mishnah question about a practice and its time — a rule-shaped opening, not a story.

Mishnah Pesachim 1:1.hebrew: אוֹר לְאַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר בּוֹדְקִין אֶת הֶחָמֵץ
Mishnah Pesachim 1:1.translation: On the eve of the fourteenth one searches for leaven.
Mishnah Pesachim 1:1.setting: A compact Mishnah case that opens with a time and an action — a question-shaped rule, not a story.

Mishnah Bava Kamma 1:1.setting: A counted Mishnah opening that names a field of cases before any one example is worked.

Mishnah Bava Metzia 1:1.translation: Two people are holding a garment.
Mishnah Bava Metzia 1:1.setting: A concrete Mishnah case: two claimants, one object — name who acts before asking the law.

Berakhot 2a.translation: On what is the tanna standing, that he teaches: “From when?”
Berakhot 2a.setting: The Gemara quotes the Mishnah’s rule-shaped opening and immediately presses it with a question.

Berakhot 2a (Vilna page).translation: From when do we recite Shema in the evening?
Berakhot 2a (Vilna page).setting: On a Vilna Talmud page this Mishnah–Gemara block sits in the center; commentary fills the columns around it.

Mishnah and Gemara, Berakhot 2a.translation: From when do we recite Shema in the evening?
Mishnah and Gemara, Berakhot 2a.setting: The Mishnah states the practice; the Gemara that follows (often marked גמ׳) begins the discussion of it.

Gemara Berakhot 2a.translation: On what is the tanna standing, that he teaches: “From when?”
Gemara Berakhot 2a.setting: A Gemara line that asks about the Mishnah’s opening rather than retelling a story.

Gemara Berakhot 2b.translation: and further · rather · as it is said.
Gemara Berakhot 2b.setting: Berakhot 2b argument signals already used in Academy orientation — adding, correcting, and citing.

Gemara Shabbat 55a.hebrew: חוֹתָמוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֱמֶת
Gemara Shabbat 55a.translation: The seal of the Holy One is truth.
Gemara Shabbat 55a.setting: A named-voice Gemara line already used in Academy middot sessions — attach the statement to its speaker.

Gemara Eruvin 13b.translation: These and those are the words of the living God.
Gemara Eruvin 13b.setting: A discussion line that holds two views open rather than closing them with a single ruling.

Gemara Sukkah 2a.hebrew: סוּכָּה שֶׁהִיא גְבוֹהָה לְמַעְלָה מֵעֶשְׂרִים אַמָּה
Gemara Sukkah 2a.translation: A sukkah that is higher than twenty cubits.
Gemara Sukkah 2a.setting: A validity case: a structure, a measure, and a ruling that later discussion may narrow.

Gemara Bava Metzia 2a.translation: Two people are holding a garment.
Gemara Bava Metzia 2a.setting: The opening case on the daf: two claimants, one object, and no proof yet of ownership.

Bava Metzia 59b.setting: From the Oven of Akhnai story — a tension the passage leaves standing rather than tidily settling.

A dispute closed with teiku.translation: Let it stand — the question is left undecided.
A dispute closed with teiku.setting: A discussion marker that closes a dispute without a verdict (as in Yoma 49a). The openness is the point, not a missing page.

Kiddushin 31b.translation: What is reverence, and what is honor?
Kiddushin 31b.setting: The Gemara cites and distinguishes two verses on honoring parents — quoted words, then the argument built on them.

Gittin 55b.translation: On account of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, Jerusalem was destroyed.
Gittin 55b.setting: A story window: a man is shamed at a feast after a mistaken invitation — state what happens before drawing a lesson.

Mikraot Gedolot, Genesis 1:1.hebrew: בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ
Mikraot Gedolot, Genesis 1:1.translation: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
Mikraot Gedolot, Genesis 1:1.setting: On a Mikraot Gedolot page the verse sits as the primary text; commentaries are printed around it.

Rashi on Genesis 1:1.hebrew: בְּרֵאשִׁית — אֵין הַמִּקְרָא הַזֶּה אוֹמֵר אֶלָּא דָּרְשֵׁנִי
Rashi on Genesis 1:1.translation: 'In the beginning' — this verse says nothing other than 'interpret me.'
Rashi on Genesis 1:1.setting: Commentary quotes a word from the verse, then explains it — the quoted-word-then-explanation shape.

Pirkei Avot 1:1.hebrew: מֹשֶׁה קִבֵּל תּוֹרָה מִסִּינַי וּמְסָרָהּ לִיהוֹשֻׁעַ
Pirkei Avot 1:1.translation: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua.
Pirkei Avot 1:1.setting: An anonymous Mishnah voice narrating a chain of transmission — no “Rabbi X said” formula on this opening line.

Pirkei Avot 1:2.hebrew: שִׁמְעוֹן הַצַּדִּיק הָיָה מִשְּׁיָרֵי כְנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה. הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר
Pirkei Avot 1:2.translation: Shimon the Righteous was of the remnants of the Great Assembly. He used to say…
Pirkei Avot 1:2.setting: A named sage plus “he used to say” — an attribution formula before the teaching itself.

Pirkei Avot 3:2.hebrew: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וְאָכַלְתָּ וְשָׂבָעְתָּ וּבֵרַכְתָּ · מִכָּאן אָמְרוּ
Pirkei Avot 3:2.translation: as it is said: “you shall eat and be satisfied and bless” · from here they said.
Pirkei Avot 3:2.setting: A teaching cites a verse, then comments — a short bound-the-quote window already used in Academy orientation.

Pirkei Avot 5:7.translation: Who is wise? One who learns from every person.
Pirkei Avot 5:7.setting: An Avot teaching already used in Academy sessions — restating it in your own words is the skill.

Amidah, opening blessing.setting: A blessing formula of public address — liturgical praise, not a legal case.

Kaddish.translation: May His great name be magnified and sanctified.
Kaddish.setting: A prayer of public praise — liturgical address, not a legal case or a Torah narrative.

Rambam, Yesodei HaTorah 1:1.hebrew: יְסוֹד הַיְסוֹדוֹת וְעַמּוּד הַחָכְמוֹת לֵידַע שֶׁיֵּשׁ שָׁם מָצוּי רִאשׁוֹן
Rambam, Yesodei HaTorah 1:1.translation: The foundation of foundations and the pillar of wisdoms is to know that there is a First Being.
Rambam, Yesodei HaTorah 1:1.setting: A code-style claim stated as a principle, not as a back-and-forth sugya.

Rambam, Hilchot Deot 1:4.hebrew: הַדֶּרֶךְ הַיְשָׁרָה הִיא מִדָּה בֵינוֹנִית · לְפִיכָךְ צִוּוּ חֲכָמִים
Rambam, Hilchot Deot 1:4.translation: The straight way is the middle measure; therefore the sages commanded.
Rambam, Hilchot Deot 1:4.setting: A code-style principle about character — a "therefore" connector draws a conclusion in legal prose, not in a back-and-forth discussion.

Rambam, Hilchot Deot 1:5.setting: A code line that can grant a point and then adjust the original claim — already used in Academy character sessions.

Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 1:1.hebrew: יִתְגַּבֵּר כָּאֲרִי לַעֲמוֹד בַּבֹּקֶר לַעֲבוֹדַת בּוֹרְאוֹ
Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 1:1.translation: One should strengthen oneself like a lion to rise in the morning to serve his Creator.
Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 1:1.setting: A code-style line that states what to do — it closes options rather than weighing several views.

Orchot Tzaddikim.setting: Mussar names a trait, then works a case of someone who… — a short middah window already used in Academy sessions.

Guide for the Perplexed.translation: Permission / freedom is given to every person.
Guide for the Perplexed.setting: A Maimonidean philosophical line already used in Academy thought sessions — it states a difficulty, then the work answers it.

One passage with a ruling and a story si.hebrew: חָרוּב · בַּת קוֹל · לֹא בַשָּׁמַיִם הִיא · נִצְּחוּנִי בָנַי
One passage with a ruling and a story si.translation: Carob tree · Heavenly Voice · it is not in heaven · My children have defeated Me.
One passage with a ruling and a story si.setting: One sugya holds a legal principle beside a story — read the ruling for practice, the story for meaning.

Psalm vs. legal code.hebrew: ה׳ רֹעִי לֹא אֶחְסָר · יְסוֹד הַיְסוֹדוֹת
Psalm vs. legal code.translation: The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not lack. · The foundation of foundations…
Psalm vs. legal code.setting: A psalm line of image beside a code-style claim — poetry invites resonance; a code invites precision.

A source with several undecided views.translation: These and those are the words of the living God.
A source with several undecided views.setting: A source that lays out more than one view and does not by itself tell you what to do.

A code of Jewish law with disagreeing ex.hebrew: אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים וַהֲלָכָה כְּבֵית הִלֵּל
A code of Jewish law with disagreeing ex.translation: These and those are the words of the living God — and the halakha follows Beit Hillel.
A code of Jewish law with disagreeing ex.setting: A later line that both preserves disagreement and states a practice — studying it is not yet a personal ruling.

A source of Jewish law studied on your o.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
A source of Jewish law studied on your o.setting: Study yields understanding, not a personal ruling — a boundary window already used in Academy halakha sessions.
